articles.title: We brought back the lynx, but will we save the rest?
articles.excerpt: When Portuguese biologist Henrique Pereira was a kid in the 1980s, there were almost no vultures left in southern Europe. Now, “you cannot drive more than a few days in Portugal or Spain without seeing vultures flying over,” he told The European Correspondent. “There was a huge recovery.” The professor of biodiversity conservation at the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg told The European Correspondent about the success stories of European wildlife recovery: bears, lynxes, and wolves, for example. Wildlife that was once close to extinction made a comeback. A new WWF report looks into global wildlife loss and paints a less pretty picture: the size of global vertebrate wildlife populations has shrunk by an average of 73% since 1970. articles.title: The fungal networks hiding beneath our feet
articles.excerpt: Something massive is hiding underground: large networks of tiny threads, each many times thinner than a hair. If laid out end to end, they would stretch about 110 quadrillion kilometres – roughly 730 million times the distance from Earth to the sun. These tiny threads are fungi, specifically mycorrhizal fungi. You may think of fungi as mushrooms, but these ones live mostly underground. “Underneath your foot, you might have hundreds of metres of these fungal threads,” Justin Stewart, an evolutionary ecologist and postdoctoral fellow at the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), told us. Stewart is the lead author of a recent study published in Science, used by SPUN to create the first-ever global map of mycorrhizal fungi. These fungi are fantastic biological partners to plants. articles.title: Who pays for pricier carbon? You, until the help arrives
articles.excerpt: If you heat your home and fill up your car with gas, oil, or coal, your bills are likely going up from 2028. The EU’s new carbon pricing system, the Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2), will make fossil fuel suppliers pay for the emissions from the fuel they sell, and they’ll pass that cost on to you. For most households, the increase in heating costs will be modest at around €60 a year on average, according to estimates from the Bertelsmann Foundation. But in Poland, households heating with oil, gas, or coal could pay €372 more each year. The hardest hit are often older homeowners in Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Poland, living on around half the average income in their countries. articles.title: Good news for the planet, bad news for Norway
articles.excerpt: Norway has a green reputation, but it's one of the world's largest exporters of oil and gas, and the EU is its main customer. That could change: the EU is upholding a ban on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, despite heavy lobbying from Oslo. Norway has become the Union’s largest gas supplier since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, providing roughly a third of its imports. Most of that gas comes from the North Sea, but some already flows from the Arctic, where Norway has produced gas since 2007 and opened its northernmost oil field last year. The country's production is forecast to decline after 2027 unless new reserves are found, most of which are expected in the northern Barents Sea. articles.title: We can still refreeze the climate ice cube
articles.excerpt: “If you take an ice cube out of the freezer and put it on the table, it starts to melt. If you put the ice cube back in the freezer quick enough, it will freeze again,” climate scientist Nico Wunderling tells me. “But if you wait too long, it will melt entirely before you put it back, and you can’t put the water back into the cube form.” He’s explaining climate tipping points, his area of research at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Goethe University Frankfurt. Tipping points are thresholds where a small rise in warming triggers a self-reinforcing feedback loop that becomes very hard to reverse. Think of the melting Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets as giant versions of the melting ice cube. articles.title: Europe promised to ban cages, but industry got the biggest say
articles.excerpt: Each year, more than 300 million farm animals in the EU live in cages. Europeans overwhelmingly want that to change: 84% think the welfare of farmed animals should be improved, and 60% are even willing to pay more for it, according to a 2023 Eurobarometer survey. The European Food Safety Authority also recommends avoiding the use of cages for broiler chickens and laying hens to improve animal health and welfare. In 2021, the European Commission committed to ending caged farming following the European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) “End the Cage Age”, which gathered more than 1.4 million signatures and support from over 170 organisations for a complete ban on cages for farmed animals.
